name: Mjölnir
powers: Summons thunder and lightning; returns to the thrower's hand; hallows weddings and funerals.
description: Mjölnir, 'the grinder', is the war-hammer of the thunder god Thor, forged by the dwarven brothers Brokkr and Sindri as the prize of a wager Loki placed on his own head. Because Loki, in the shape of a fly, bit the smith's hand while he worked the bellows, the hammer's handle came out too short — which is why Thor wields it with one hand. The Prose Edda counts it among the god's three great treasures, beside the belt Megingjörð and the iron gloves Járngreipr; its head is sometimes said to be iron and the shaft wooden, and the hammer returns to the thrower's hand like a boomerang after striking. Beyond battle it hallows marriages, births, funerals, ships, and fields, and it will be the weapon with which Thor fells Jörmungandr at Ragnarök. Small iron and silver hammer pendants of the Viking Age, such as the figure from Eyrarland, are widely read as images of Mjölnir worn for protection. It remains the most recognised symbol of Norse paganism and is still used as a badge of identity in modern heathen communities.

name: Gungnir
powers: Never misses its mark; its throwers and possession pledge a solemn oath.
description: Gungnir, 'the swaying one', is the spear of Odin, the All-Father, forged by the dwarven sons of Ivaldi in the same contest of treasures that gave the gods their greatest gifts. In the Prose Edda the spear is listed as one of the three marvels the sons of Ivaldi made — the others being Skíðblaðnir and Sif's golden hair. The All-Father opened the war between the Æsir and the Vanir by hurling Gungnir over the enemy host, and that gesture of casting a spear at the start of a battle became the archetype for the practice in Old Norse and later Germanic warfare. Oaths sworn on Gungnir, often called the 'spear-oath', were held to be unbreakable, and the name was used in skaldic kennings as a kenning for 'spear' or 'weapon'. At Ragnarök Odin rides against the wolf Fenrir armed with the spear, though the weapon cannot save him. Gungnir remains a byword for Odin's authority and appears constantly in art and fiction that draws on Norse myth.

name: Draupnir
powers: Drips eight equal rings every ninth night.
description: Draupnir, 'the dripper', is the golden ring of Odin, forged by the dwarven brothers Brokkr and Sindri in the same wager that produced Mjölnir. Every ninth night, eight rings of equal weight drip from it, making it an endless source of gold and a symbol of abundance. When Baldr was laid on his funeral ship Hringhorni, Odin placed Draupnir on the pyre; the ring was later fetched back from Hel by Baldr's brother Hermóðr, who rode the eight-legged horse Sleipnir to the underworld at Frigg's bidding. In that story Hermóðr returns to the gods bearing Draupnir and the gifts that the dead send back to the living — Nanna's linen robe for Frigg and a ring for the goddess Fulla. The ring's self-replicating nature has made it one of the most studied of the dwarven treasures, and its name is sometimes used in modern writing as a shorthand for limitless wealth.

name: Skíðblaðnir
powers: Folds up like a cloth into a pocket; always has a fair wind.
description: Skíðblaðnir is the best of all ships, built for the god Freyr by the dwarven sons of Ivaldi and listed among their marvels in the Prose Edda. It is large enough to carry all the gods and their weapons, yet it can be folded up like a cloth and carried in a pouch when not in use. The ship always finds a fair wind wherever it sails, so the gods never lack for a swift voyage, and it is sometimes said to be made of wood thin enough to fold without breaking. In Snorri's account the ship is counted as one of the greatest treasures of the gods, and it also sails the company of the gods at Ragnarök in some retellings. Though no physical counterpart survives, the name has lived on in Scandinavian shipping and fiction as a byword for a perfect, always-favorable vessel.

name: Brísingamen
powers: Heightens the beauty of its wearer; a treasure of the goddess Freyja.
description: Brísingamen, the necklace of the goddess Freyja, is one of the great treasures of the Norse gods, forged by the dwarves. The Prose Edda lists it among the wealth of the gods, and in the poem Lokasenna Loki taunts Freyja that she had to sleep with each of the four dwarves who made it to obtain it — a story expanded in the later Sörla þáttr, where Freyja is described as bartering her favours for the jewel. The necklace is also central to the legend of the hero Þórólfr and to the tale of the god Heimdallr and Loki, who fought over it in the shape of seals at Singasteinn; Heimdallr recovered it for Freyja. The name is sometimes taken to mean 'bright' or 'gleaming' necklace, and the jewel later became a model for Freyja's shining golden hair of amber. Brísingamen remains a standard example of the dwarven treasure hoard in retellings of Norse myth.

name: Gleipnir
powers: Unbreakable binding that holds the wolf Fenrir until Ragnarök.
description: Gleipnir is the third and final fetter with which the gods bound the wolf Fenrir, after the great chains Leyding and Drómi both snapped. It was made by the dwarves from six impossible things: the sound of a cat's footfall, a woman's beard, the roots of a mountain, a bear's sinews, a fish's breath, and a bird's spittle — which is why, the Edda explains, none of these things now exist in the world. Gleipnir is as thin as a silken ribbon, yet nothing could break it. To persuade the suspicious wolf to let himself be bound, the god Týr placed his hand in Fenrir's mouth as a pledge, and lost it when the wolf found himself unable to escape. The binding holds until Ragnarök, when the wolf breaks free in the final battle. Gleipnir is the classic example of the 'impossible object' in Old Norse mythology.

name: Andvaranaut
powers: Cursed to bring death and misfortune to every possessor after the dwarf who made it.
description: Andvaranaut is the ring at the heart of the cursed gold of the dwarf Andvari, taken from him by Loki at the waterfall Gnitaheiðr after the god caught the dwarf in the shape of a pike. When Andvari was forced to give up his treasure hoard, he kept a single ring, and when Loki wrenched that away too, the dwarf laid a curse on the gold: it would destroy every possessor who came after him. The treasure passed to the chieftain Hreiðmarr as wergild for his murdered son Otr, then to the dragon Fáfnir, and finally to the hero Sigurðr, and ruin followed each owner. The story is told in the Völsunga saga and echoed in the Middle High German Nibelungenlied, and Andvaranaut is widely seen as the direct ancestor of the Ring of the Nibelung in Richard Wagner's opera cycle. Its name, 'Andvari's gift', has become shorthand for a treasure that brings only doom.

name: Gram
maker: Reforged by Regin from the shards of Sigmund's blade
powers: Slices through a smith's anvil and the body of the dragon Fáfnir.
description: Gram is the great sword of the Völsung heroes, first owned by Sigmund and later reforged for his son Sigurðr, the slayer of the dragon Fáfnir. The sword enters the story when Odin, disguised as a wanderer, thrusts it into the great tree Branstock in the hall of King Völsung, declaring that the one who draws it shall have it as a gift; only Sigmund could pull the blade free. When the sword broke in battle, the shards were kept and re-forged by the smith Regin, and Sigurðr proved the new blade by laying it on the anvil and cleaving it in two before using it to kill Fáfnir. In the German tradition the same sword is called Nothung in the Nibelungenlied and Balmung in other versions, and it lives on in Wagner's Ring cycle as Siegfried's reforged sword. Gram is therefore one of the most famous swords in all of Germanic legend.

name: Megingjörð
powers: Doubles the god's already godlike strength.
description: Megingjörð, the 'might-girdle', is the belt of the thunder god Thor, and the Prose Edda names it as one of his three great treasures together with the hammer Mjölnir and the iron gloves Járngreipr. When Thor girds the belt about his waist his already godlike strength is doubled, so that no giant can stand against him in the wrestling-matches and battle-tales of the Eddas. In the tale of Thor's journey to the giant Geirröðr, the giantess Gríðr lends the god a similar belt of might along with her staff, showing that such power-girdles were a fixed part of the mythic image of the thunder god. The belt is sometimes said to be made of leather with a heavy buckle, though the sources give no detailed description of its form. Megingjörð survives in modern retellings as the standard third element of Thor's arsenal, and its name is a stock kenning-adjacent byword for supernatural strength.

name: Járngreipr
powers: Let Thor grip the white-hot shaft of Mjölnir.
description: Járngreipr, the 'iron grippers', are the iron gloves of the thunder god Thor, named in the Prose Edda as one of his three great treasures beside Mjölnir and the belt Megingjörð. Their purpose is practical as much as martial: the shaft of Mjölnir is said to grow white-hot in flight, and only the iron gloves let Thor catch and hurl the hammer without burning his hands. In the tale of Thor's visit to the giant Geirröðr, gloves of the same kind are what allow the god to catch the red-hot lump of molten iron that the giant throws at him, which Thor hurls back to kill Geirröðr. The gloves are sometimes said to have been forged by the dwarves, though the Edda does not name their maker. Járngreipr appears in most modern retellings of Norse myth as the practical complement to the great hammer.

name: Naglfar
material: Untrimmed fingernails and toenails of the dead
powers: Bear the forces of chaos from the east across the waters at Ragnarök.
description: Naglfar, the 'nail-ship', is the great ship of the dead in Norse mythology, built from the untrimmed fingernails and toenails of the dead. The Prose Edda warns that the ship is always under construction, and that the dead should therefore be buried with clipped nails — every unclipped nail added to the awful ship. At Ragnarök Naglfar sails from the east carrying the forces of chaos across the waters: in the poem Völuspá the giant Hrym steers it, while Snorri places Loki at the helm, and the ship bears the host of frost giants toward the battlefield of Vígríðr. The galleon of the dead is one of the most striking images of the end of the world in Old Norse literature, and the practical folk-custom of trimming nails for the sake of delaying the ship's completion kept the myth alive in daily life. Naglfar remains a standard image in retellings of Ragnarök and in art inspired by Norse mythology.

name: Hliðskjálf
powers: From it the sitter can see across all the worlds.
description: Hliðskjálf is the high seat of Odin in Valhöll, from which the All-Father can see across all the worlds and watch everything that happens among gods, men, and giants. The Prose Edda describes it as a throne of far-seeing power, and both Odin and, at times, his wife Frigg use it to scan the cosmos. Sitting in it unbidden was dangerous: the god Freyr once took the seat, was struck by a sight of the giantess Gerðr in the distance, and fell so hopelessly in love that he sent his servant Skírnir to woo her, giving away his own magic sword as payment — the sword whose loss later costs Freyr his life at Ragnarök. The name appears in Skírnismál and throughout the Eddas, and the throne has become the standard image of Odin's all-seeing kingship over the nine worlds.

name: Gjallarhorn
powers: Its sound carries across all the worlds; it calls the gods to the final battle.
description: Gjallarhorn is the great horn of Heimdallr, the watchman of the gods who guards the rainbow bridge Bifröst, and its sound carries across all the worlds. At Ragnarök Heimdallr raises the horn to his lips and its blast summons gods and men to the final battle on the field of Vígríðr, a call that is among the great set-pieces of Norse eschatology. Snorri also says that Heimdallr drinks from the horn at the well of Mímir, suggesting that it doubled as a drinking vessel in some accounts. The name 'resounding horn' or 'shrill horn' fits its role as the signal of the end times. Gjallarhorn has passed into modern culture as the archetype of a world-ending call, and it appears in fantasy fiction, music, and art whenever the Ragnarök myth is retold.

name: Hringhorni
powers: The greatest of ships, large enough to bear a god's funeral pyre.
description: Hringhorni is the greatest of all ships, the vessel on which the gods laid the body of Baldr the Beautiful after his death by the mistletoe dart. When the gods tried to launch Hringhorni for the funeral, the ship was so heavy that no god or giant could move it, until the giantess Hyrrokkin came riding on a wolf and sent the vessel sliding into the sea with a single shove, the earth shaking with the force. The funeral of Baldr, with the pyre lit on the ship, the ring Draupnir laid upon it, and the dwarf Litr cast into the flames, is one of the most famous scenes in the Prose Edda. The name is sometimes taken to mean 'ring-prowed' or 'ship with a ring-shaped stern'. Hringhorni appears in skaldic references and remains a fixed image in retellings of Baldr's death.

name: Ægishjálmr
powers: Strikes fear into enemies and grants the wearer protection in battle.
description: Ægishjálmr, the 'helm of awe' or 'helm of terror', is a protective sign of Norse and Icelandic tradition, drawn as a wheel of radiating prongs or staves. In the poem Fáfnismál the dragon Fáfnir is said to have worn the helm of awe, and the hero Sigurðr takes it as part of the dragon's hoard, suggesting a literal helmet in the oldest layer of the story. From the early modern period the name came to be attached to an eight-armed magical stave of the Icelandic galdrabækur, drawn on the forehead between the brows or on the brow of a person to strike fear into enemies and give victory and protection; the 17th-century grimoire tradition is where the familiar branched symbol comes from. The two uses are sometimes confused, and it is likely the modern stave design and the Eddic helmet are different things that share a name. Ægishjálmr remains one of the most reproduced of all Icelandic staves, in tattoos, jewellery, and fantasy art.

name: Vegvísir
powers: Guides the bearer safely through storms and unknown lands.
description: Vegvísir, the 'wayfinder', is an Icelandic magical stave drawn as a central point with radiating runic spokes, first attested in the Huld manuscript, compiled by Geir Vigfússon at Akureyri in 1860. The accompanying text promises that whoever carries the sign will never lose their way in storm or bad weather, even when the path is unknown, and the stave is drawn on paper, wood, or metal and carried as a talisman. Although it is often called a 'Viking compass', the earliest known source is a 19th-century grimoire, and the symbol has no confirmed Viking-Age counterpart — a point that popular culture frequently overlooks. Vegvísir has become the most widely reproduced of all the galdrastafir, appearing in tattoos, jewellery, and merchandise, and the Museum of Icelandic Sorcery at Hólmavík displays it among the living folk-magic tradition.

name: Gallehus Golden Horns
maker: Maker named in runic inscription: LagestheR
powers: Ceremonial drinking and ritual horns; images thought to invoke protection and fertility.
description: The Gallehus golden horns are two magnificent drinking and ritual horns of the 5th century AD, found in a field at Gallehus in southern Jutland in 1639 and 1734 and among the most famous objects of Nordic antiquity. The shorter horn bore a Proto-Norse runic inscription along the rim, 'ek hlewagastiR holtijaR horna tawido' — 'I, Hlewagastir (also read as LagestheR) of Holt, made the horn' — one of the earliest complete sentences written in the Elder Futhark. Both horns were built up from rings of sheet gold covered with stamped and soldered figures of men, beasts, and symbols, whose meaning scholars still debate. In 1802 they were stolen from the Royal Kunstkammer and melted down by the goldsmith Niels Heidenreich, an act that made the horns a national tragedy in Denmark; reconstructions made from the surviving 18th-century drawings are displayed at the National Museum in Copenhagen, and the horns inspired Oehlenschläger's poem 'Guldhornene'.

name: The Sunken Church Bell
powers: Said to ring from beneath the water on holy nights, and to be recoverable only by one pure of heart.
description: The sunken church bell is a recurring folk motif of Sweden and the wider Nordic region: a church bell that lies lost in a lake or river, usually because it sank while being ferried to a church or was dragged down by a troll or the water-folk who hated its ringing. The bell is sometimes said to toll faintly beneath the surface on Christmas night or other holy nights, and treasure-hunters who try to raise it are said to glimpse it and then watch it slip away again, unless a pure-hearted person can win it. The legend is told in many local variants across Sweden, Norway, and Finland, often tied to named lakes and parishes. It also echoes a real custom, since church bells were occasionally lost in transport. The motif survives in place-lore, folk music, and children's stories as one of the most beloved lake legends of the north.

name: Troll's Gift Ring
powers: Gifts from the hidden folk bring luck to those who accept them without greed, and ruin to the grasping.
description: The troll's gift ring belongs to a widespread Nordic belief that the hidden folk — the huldra, the hill-folk, and the trolls — sometimes press gifts upon humans: rings, bracelets, belts, or coins that gleam like gold. In the folk tradition it is said that a person who accepted such a gift courteously and without greed could keep lasting luck, while one who snatched greedily at more, or refused rudely, would be cursed with misfortune; at dawn the fine gift might also be found to have turned to leaves, moss, or ashes, the standard fate of fairy gold. The motif is told across Norway, Sweden, and Denmark with many local variations, and it belongs to the wider Scandinavian lore of encounters with the underworld folk rather than to any single saga. The custom of the gift-ring illustrates the deep belief that luck in this world hung on how one treated the hidden neighbours.
source: Norwegian folk tradition (eventyr and sagn collections)

name: Sampo
powers: Grinds out grain, salt, and gold for its possessor.
description: The Sampo is the wonder-working mill of Finnish epic, forged by the great smith Ilmarinen as the bride-price demanded for the hand of the maiden of Pohjola. In the Kalevala the Sampo grinds out limitless grain, salt, and gold for its possessor, making it the engine of the northern world's wealth. The heroes of Väinölä and Louhi, the mistress of Pohjola, fight over it in the great raid that follows; during the sea-battle the Sampo is shattered and lost overboard, and the fragments that wash ashore are said to have given the sea and the land of Finland their richness. Its true shape and nature are never fully described — it is a mill, a chest, a pillar, or simply 'the Sampo' — and scholars still debate what it originally was. It stands as the central object of the Kalevala, and its name lives on in Finnish art, music, and the Finnish word for a lucky wonder.

name: Tyrfing
aliases: The Cursed Sword of Hervarar saga
powers: Never misses and never rusts, but kills a man every time it is drawn and brings three great evils.
description: Tyrfing is the cursed sword of the Hervarar saga, forged by the dwarves Dvalinn and Dulinn for King Svafrlami. When the king forced the dwarves to give him the finest blade they could make, they laid a curse upon it in return: the sword would never miss a stroke, never rust, would kill a man every time it was drawn, and would be the cause of three great evils. After killing the dwarves, Svafrlami was himself slain in a duel with the berserk Arngrímr, and the blade passed into the hands of Arngrímr's sons. The shield-maiden Hervör later raised the sword from the barrow of her dead father Angantýr by overcoming his ghost, and the curse drove the saga's later heroes, including Heiðrekr, to their deaths. Tyrfing is one of the archetypal cursed blades of Germanic legend and is often compared with Sigurðr's Gram.

name: Óðrœrir
aliases: The Kettle of the Mead of Poetry
powers: Holds the mead of poetry; whoever drinks it gains poetry and wisdom.
description: Óðrœrir is the kettle that holds the mead of poetry, brewed by the dwarves Fjalar and Galar from the blood of Kvasir, the wisest of beings, mixed with honey. Whoever drinks the mead gains the gift of poetry and wisdom, and the brew is stored in three vessels — the great kettle Óðrœrir and the two bowls Boðn and Són. The giant Suttungr seized the mead after the dwarves killed his parents, and Odin stole it back from Suttungr's daughter Gunnlöð, drinking all of Óðrœrir in three draughts and escaping in eagle form. A little of the mead is said to have been spilled from Odin's beak, and that spill became the portion that is given to poets on earth. The name is sometimes interpreted as 'stirrer of inspiration' or 'mind-rousing one', and the mead remains the central symbol of skaldic poetry and of the gift of verse.

name: Sif's Golden Hair
aliases: The Gold of the Sons of Ivaldi
powers: Grows from the head like real hair and never loses its gleam.
description: Sif's golden hair is the treasure that the dwarven sons of Ivaldi made for Sif, the wife of Thor, after Loki maliciously shaved her head. To atone for his mischief Loki had the sons of Ivaldi forge hair of pure gold so fine that it grew from Sif's head like real hair, and the making of it opened the great contest of treasures in which the dwarves vied against each other — the same contest that produced Gungnir, Skíðblaðnir, Mjölnir, and Draupnir. In the Prose Edda the golden hair is listed among the gifts the sons of Ivaldi delivered, and the story explains why gold is called 'Sif's hair' in skaldic kennings. The tale shows the dwarves as the great craftsmen of the gods and Loki as the instigator of their finest work. Sif's hair remains a standard example of the dwarven gift-hoard and of gold-kennings in Old Norse poetry.

name: Gullinbursti
powers: Its golden bristles light the darkest night, and it runs through air and water faster than any horse.
description: Gullinbursti, the 'golden-bristled boar', is the boar of the god Freyr, forged by the dwarven brothers Brokkr and Sindri in the same wager that produced the hammer Mjölnir. Its bristles are of gold and shine so brightly that they light the darkest night, and the boar can run through air and water faster than any horse, drawing Freyr's chariot in place of a steed. Snorri records that Odin judged Gullinbursti the best of all the dwarves' gifts, naming the boar along with its second name Slíðrugtanni, and that Freyr rode it to Baldr's funeral. The boar is also the ancestor of the golden boar of Swedish royal imagery and of the Christmas ham that crowns the Swedish table, traditions that carry the myth quietly into modern life. Gullinbursti is one of the most beloved minor treasures of Norse mythology.

name: Freyr's Sword
aliases: The Sword That Fights by Itself
powers: Fights of its own accord, without a hand to wield it.
description: Freyr's sword is the magic blade of the god Freyr that fights by itself, without a hand to wield it. In Skírnismál, Freyr gives the sword to his servant Skírnir as payment for wooing the giantess Gerðr on his behalf — a gift of the self-fighting sword in exchange for love. The loss is fatal at Ragnarök: the Prose Edda recounts that Freyr, lacking his good sword, fights the fire giant Surtr and falls, having given away his only weapon. The sword is thus remembered in the Eddas as the price of love and the cause of a god's death, and it is often read as a parable of how love and war can demand the same sacrifice. It remains a standard example in discussions of the self-acting weapons of myth, and the tale of the sword given away for Gerðr is retold in most modern versions of the Eddas.

name: Víðarr's Shoe
aliases: The Shoe of the Silent God
material: Scrap leather gathered from all men's shoes
powers: Holds firm against Fenrir's jaws so Víðarr can tear the wolf apart at Ragnarök.
description: Víðarr's shoe is the enormous foot-covering of Víðarr, the silent son of Odin, made from the pieces of leather that people are said to have cut from their own shoes at heel and toe and set aside for the god. The Prose Edda explains that every man who wishes to help the god should donate such scraps, and the collected leather forms a shoe strong enough to hold against Fenrir's jaws. At Ragnarök the silent Víðarr sets the shoe against the wolf's lower jaw, grips the upper jaw with his hands, and tears the wolf's mouth apart, avenging the death of his father Odin. The detail of the shoe-scraps is one of the strangest and most memorable practical customs in the Eddas, and it connects the cosmic battle to the ordinary work of mending shoes. Víðarr's vengeance remains a fixed scene in every retelling of Ragnarök.

name: Drómi and Leyding
powers: Failed bindings; only the silken dwarf-made fetter Gleipnir finally held Fenrir.
description: Leyding and Drómi are the first two fetters with which the gods tried to bind the wolf Fenrir, before the silken dwarf-made fetter Gleipnir finally held him. The gods first had a great chain called Leyding forged, but the wolf snapped it as easily as a cord. They then made a second, much stronger fetter called Drómi, but when Fenrir braced his feet against the ground and braced his back against a rock, he burst the chain apart, sending fragments flying across the countryside. The two failed fetters set up the famous scene in which the suspicious wolf agreed to be bound by the 'silken ribbon' Gleipnir only if a god placed his hand in the beast's mouth as a pledge — the pledge that cost Týr his hand. Leyding and Drómi thus frame the myth of the binding of Fenrir, and the story of the chain that was too strong for its maker remains one of the best-known episodes of the Eddas.

name: Svalinn
powers: Tempering the sun's rays so the earth and sea are not consumed by fire.
description: Svalinn, 'the chill' or 'the cooling one', is the shield that stands before the sun in Norse mythology, named in the poem Grímnismál. According to the stanza, the shield protects the earth from the burning rays of the sun goddess Sól as she is dragged across the sky by the horses Árvakr and Alsviðr, and 'mountains and sea would be set in flames' if it ever fell from its place. The shield is also named in Sigrdrífumál and in Snorri's list of shield-names in Skáldskaparmál, and scholars have suggested it preserves a Bronze Age image of the sun as a round, shield-like disc. Unlike a warrior's shield, Svalinn is a world-sustaining object, and its role in keeping creation from burning up makes it one of the most purely cosmic objects in the Eddic corpus. It is sometimes cited in modern writing as an early image of solar protection.

name: Hǫfuð
powers: The sword of Heimdall, watchman of the gods, named among his possessions in the Edda.
description: Hǫfuð, meaning 'head', is the sword of Heimdallr, the watchman of the gods, named among his possessions in the Prose Edda. Snorri lists the blade beside Heimdallr's duties as guardian of the gods, and later tradition links the sword to the final battle, in which Heimdallr and Loki are said to slay one another at Ragnarök. Very little else is recorded about the weapon, and no detailed story of its forging or use survives, which makes it one of the more mysterious named swords of the Eddas. The name 'head' is sometimes explained as a kenning-like epithet for a sword, or as a reference to the head that Heimdallr and Loki were said to have fought over. Hǫfuð is nevertheless a fixture in catalogues of Norse mythic weapons, even though its owner's story is told almost entirely through other objects.

name: Lævateinn
maker: Unnamed (forged with rune magic in some readings)
powers: The only weapon said able to slay the rooster Viðófnir at the top of the world tree.
description: Lævateinn, the 'wounding wand', is the blade of the poem Fjölsvinnsmál, the only weapon said to be able to slay the rooster Viðófnir that perches at the top of the world tree. The wand lies in a chest beside the giantess Sinmara, bound by nine locks that can be opened only by a feather plucked from Viðófnir's own tail, a riddle-like condition that keeps the weapon out of reach. Scholars debate whether the name means 'wounding-wand' and whether the blade is to be identified with Loki's sword, since the name in the manuscripts may be a late emendation of 'Hævateinn', the 'high-wand'. The weapon's place in the late, riddling poem Fjölsvinnsmál sets it apart from the better-known Eddic swords. Lævateinn is nonetheless a favourite of catalogue-writers and of modern fantasy that draws on Old Norse weaponry.

name: Gríðarvölr
powers: A staff of might lent to Thor, with which he slew the giant Geirröðr.
description: Gríðarvölr is the staff of the giantess Gríðr, mother of Víðarr, which she lent to Thor along with iron gloves and a belt of might when he set out against the giant Geirröðr. In the tale told in Skáldskaparmál, Thor uses the staff to fend off the giantess Gjálp and her kin and to brace himself when Geirröðr's sons try to crush him in a chair, and he finally breaks the giant's back with the aid of the borrowed gear. The loan is a rare act of kindness by a giantess toward the thunder god, and Gríðr is remembered as the wisest and most generous of the giantesses for it. The story shows that even Thor needed the help of the giants' own world to defeat the greatest of their kind. Gríðarvölr appears in most modern retellings of the tale of Thor's visit to Geirröðr.

name: Freyja's Falcon Cloak
powers: Lets its wearer fly in the shape of a falcon.
description: Freyja's falcon cloak, also called the feather cloak or fjaðrhamr, is a garment of feathers that lets its wearer fly in the shape of a falcon. In the Prose Edda the cloak is kept by the goddess Freyja and lent out when the gods need swift flight: Loki borrows it to search for the goddess Iðunn after the giant Þjazi carries her off, and later uses it to pursue Þjazi, who had taken the shape of an eagle, back to the walls of Asgard where the gods kill him. In the poem Þrymskviða, Freyja's cloak is likewise the means by which Loki flies out to steal back the hammer Mjölnir. Shape-shifting feather-cloaks appear elsewhere in Norse legend, most famously in the story of the smith Völund and his swan-maiden bride. Freyja's falcon cloak is the standard example of the feathered flying garment of Norse myth.

name: Nábrók
maker: Made by the wearer from a dead man's lower body
powers: Said to keep the wearer's purse from ever running empty.
description: Nábrók, the 'corpse breeches' or necropants, is a garment of Icelandic folk magic made from the skin of a dead man's lower body. According to the tradition recorded by Jón Árnason and still told today, the wearer first made a pact with a living friend that if either died, the survivor might flay the dead man's skin from the waist down; the intact skin was then worn like trousers, becoming one with the wearer's own body. To activate the charm, a coin had to be stolen from a poor widow on a great festival day and placed in the scrotum of the pants, which would then constantly draw money from the living so that the purse never ran empty. The pants had to be passed on before the wearer's death, leg by leg to a new owner, or the corpse would be swarmed with lice. A famous reproduction hangs in the Museum of Icelandic Sorcery at Hólmavík.

name: Draumstafir
powers: Drawn so the sleeper receives good or revealing dreams.
description: Draumstafir, the 'dream staves', is an Icelandic magical stave recorded in the Huld manuscript, compiled by Geir Vigfússon at Akureyri in 1860, and drawn so that the sleeper receives good or revealing dreams. It belongs to the family of galdrastafir, the sigils of the Icelandic grimoire tradition that developed between the 16th and 19th centuries, and it was drawn on paper or carved on wood and placed with the sleeper or worn about the person. The drawing instructions vary between manuscripts, and the sign is one of the many staves collected by 19th-century antiquaries from a folk-magic tradition that was already fading. In modern times draumstafir is widely reproduced in books, jewellery, and tattoos, and the Museum of Icelandic Sorcery at Hólmavík presents such staves as living expressions of Icelandic folk belief. Its simple promise — sound sleep and meaningful dreams — keeps it among the more popular of the recorded staves.

name: Kaupaloki
powers: Brings success and fair fortune in buying and selling.
description: Kaupaloki, the 'trade-luck stave', is an Icelandic magical sign recorded in the Huld manuscript, compiled by Geir Vigfússon at Akureyri in 1860, and drawn for success in buying and selling. Merchants and farmers drew or carved the stave so that bargains would turn in their favour, a piece of practical magic in a seafaring and trading society where a fair deal was a matter of survival. It belongs to the group of luck-giving galdrastafir, distinct from the protective and aggressive staves of the same grimoires, and it was carried on paper, wood, or metal when goods went to market. Like most of the staves, its earliest known source is a 19th-century collection of older material, and it is now reproduced in books and on jewellery as an emblem of Icelandic folk magic. The Museum of Icelandic Sorcery at Hólmavík keeps the trade staves among its displays of the everyday uses of magic.

name: Pungastafur
powers: Keeps the bearer's purse heavy and money from running short.
description: Pungastafur, the 'purse stave', is an Icelandic magical sign recorded in the Huld manuscript, compiled by Geir Vigfússon at Akureyri in 1860, and drawn so that money would not run short and the bearer's purse would stay heavy. It is one of the most sought-after of the money-and-luck galdrastafir, a domestic charm against poverty in a subsistence economy, drawn on paper and carried about the person or carved on a coin-purse. The name itself speaks to its purpose: 'pungi' is the Icelandic word for purse or scrotum, so the stave works on the same idea as the money-magic of the necropants, keeping the bearer's wealth sealed in. It belongs to the same family as Kaupaloki and the other luck staves, and its earliest known source is the 19th-century Huld manuscript. The purse stave remains popular in modern reproductions of Icelandic staves as a symbol of financial protection.

name: Smjörstafur
powers: Brings success in making butter.
description: Smjörstafur, the 'butter stave', is an Icelandic magical sign recorded in the Huld manuscript, compiled by Geir Vigfússon at Akureyri in 1860, and drawn or carved to bring success in making butter. In an agrarian world where dairy was wealth, a charm for a full churn was practical magic, and the stave sits among the agricultural signs recorded beside the luck, protection, and money staves of the grimoires. It was probably drawn on the churn itself or on a paper carried with the dairy work, though the sources give little detail of its use. Like all the galdrastafir, its earliest known source is a 19th-century manuscript that collected older folk-magic material, and it is now reproduced in books and on merchandise as part of the Icelandic stave revival. The butter stave is a good example of how the stave tradition reached into the humblest household work.

name: Þjófastafur
powers: Protects livestock and goods from thieves.
description: Þjófastafur, the 'thief stave', is an Icelandic magical sign recorded in the Huld manuscript, compiled by Geir Vigfússon at Akureyri in 1860, and drawn to guard livestock and goods against theft. The name literally means 'thief-stave', and the sign was meant to make a thief unable to take what belonged to the bearer, or to bring him back to face the community. It answered a real fear on isolated farmsteads, where herds and household goods had no other defence against thieves and wanderers. It belongs to the protective family of galdrastafir, and like most of the staves it is known from a 19th-century manuscript that preserved older folk tradition rather than from any Viking-Age source. The thief stave is still reproduced in books and on jewellery, and the Museum of Icelandic Sorcery at Hólmavík displays it among the protective signs of the grimoire tradition.

name: Óttastafur
powers: Strikes fear into those against whom it is used.
description: Óttastafur, the 'fear stave', is an Icelandic magical sign recorded in the Huld manuscript, compiled by Geir Vigfússon at Akureyri in 1860, and drawn to strike fear into others. As a weapon of psychological magic it was meant to cow rivals or enemies without a single blow, so that the bearer's will prevailed and opponents lost heart. It is one of the aggressive galdrastafir, sitting in the same grimoires as the protective and luck-giving staves and showing that the stave tradition served harm as readily as help. Its earliest known source is a 19th-century manuscript that collected older folk-magic material, and like the other fear signs it is now reproduced in modern books and on tattoos. The fear stave is a reminder that Icelandic folk magic was a two-edged craft, used as often to intimidate as to defend.

name: Bjargástafur
powers: Carries the bearer through danger and hardship unharmed.
description: Bjargástafur, the 'rescue stave' or 'saving stave', is an Icelandic magical sign recorded in the Huld manuscript, compiled by Geir Vigfússon at Akureyri in 1860, and drawn so that the bearer could escape or survive any danger. Its name derives from the verb bjarga, 'to save', and the grimoire tradition promises that no misfortune could hold a person who bore it, whether on land, at sea, or in a dispute. It is one of the general talismans of protection in Icelandic folk magic, carried on paper, carved on wood, or worn on the person in times of peril. Like all the galdrastafir, its earliest known source is a 19th-century manuscript that gathered older material, and it is now widely reproduced in books and on jewellery. The rescue stave remains popular today as a general symbol of safety and deliverance.

name: Ginfaxi
powers: Turns the luck of a rival or competitor, so the bearer wins the contest.
description: Ginfaxi is an Icelandic magical stave recorded in the Huld manuscript, compiled by Geir Vigfússon at Akureyri in 1860, and drawn to ensure victory over a rival in a contest or argument. In the tradition it is used together with the stave Gapaldur: Gapaldur is kept under the heel of the right foot and Ginfaxi under the toes of the left foot, so that the wearer wins bouts of Icelandic wrestling, glíma, and other competitions. The name echoes the horse-names of Norse myth such as Skinfaxi and Hrímfaxi, and a horse called Ginfaxi is attested in the sagas, though the stave itself is a folk-magic sign rather than a mythic beast. It belongs to the combative family of galdrastafir, used when the prize was a bout, a trade, or a court case. The stave is still reproduced in modern collections of Icelandic magical signs.
